# Berkeley Networking Tracker

A private, secure contact tracker for the people you want to stay connected with at Berkeley — who they are, where you met them, what they do, and how much of a priority the relationship is. Every visitor signs in with their own account, and every row in the database is invisible to everyone except the person who created it, enforced by Postgres itself (not application code).

**Live app:** https://berkeley-network-tracker-sandy.vercel.app
**Repo:** https://github.com/kureemn/berkeley-network-tracker

text:
## Features

- Email/password sign up, sign in, and sign out (Neon Managed Better Auth)
- Add a contact with name, company, role, where you met them, notes, and priority
- Priority is restricted to `high` / `medium` / `low` — enforced in Postgres, not just the UI
- Sortable, filterable contact table (click a column header to sort; filter by priority; free-text search) with a stacked-card layout on mobile
- Edit and delete your own contacts
- Contacts persist in Postgres and survive a browser refresh
- Empty names and invalid priority values are rejected with a clear, inline error message
- Distinct loading, empty, success, and error states throughout
- Fully responsive: usable on a phone as well as a desktop

## Technology stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, React 19) | File-based routing and a client-heavy App Router app were enough to keep "frontend" and "backend" cleanly separated (see [Architecture](#architecture)) without inventing a second server for a project this size. |
| Styling / components | Tailwind CSS v4 + shadcn/ui (Radix primitives) | A real component system (Dialog, Select, Table, Badge, Toast, …) instead of hand-rolled UI — accessible out of the box and easy to theme, which satisfies the "design or component system" requirement without pulling in a heavier design framework. |
| Database | Neon Postgres | Serverless Postgres with branching, and the only backend the assignment's auth/data stack is built on. |
| Auth | Neon Managed Better Auth | Hosted email/password auth that issues JWTs Postgres can read directly via `auth.user_id()` — no separate auth server to run or secrets to manage beyond a cookie secret we don't even need (see below). |

| Data access | Neon Data API (`@neondatabase/neon-js`) | A PostgREST-style REST API in front of Postgres, callable straight from the browser, with Postgres Row Level Security as the actual security boundary. This is the specific SDK the assignment calls for, used via its "two-URL object form" for both auth and data. |

title: Berkeley Network Tracker README
heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Architecture
text:
- **Frontend**: Next.js client components (everything under `app/` and `components/`). This is a deliberately "thin" frontend — it renders UI and validates input for instant feedback, but holds no privileged credentials and makes no authorization decisions itself.
- **Backend**: Neon's Managed Better Auth service (issues signed JWTs on sign-in) and the Neon Data API (a hosted PostgREST-compatible REST API that validates those JWTs and executes SQL against Postgres). This is a genuinely separate service/infrastructure from the Next.js app — the browser talks to it directly over the two public URLs below, and it is the only thing that can reach Postgres.
- **Database**: Neon Postgres. The `contacts` table, its `CHECK` constraints, and its Row Level Security policies are the actual, non-bypassable enforcement point for both data validity and per-user privacy — see the next two sections.
- **Authentication**: Managed Better Auth. `lib/neon/client.ts` builds one `NeonClient` with `createClient({ auth: { url }, dataApi: { url } })` — the "two-URL object form" — which the whole app imports as a singleton and uses for both `client.auth.*` and `client.from('contacts').*`.

title: Berkeley Network Tracker README
heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Architecture
text:
- **Hosting**: Vercel, deployed straight from the `main` branch of the GitHub repo.

Two Next.js server files exist only as thin wiring, not as a data-access layer: `next.config.ts` (Turbopack config) and `app/layout.tsx` (shared shell). There is no custom `app/api/*` proxy for contacts — every contacts request goes straight from the browser to the Neon Data API, which is safe precisely because RLS decides what each request is allowed to see or change, not the client.

## Local setup

Requires Node.js 20.9+ and a Neon account with a project that has the Data API + Managed Better Auth enabled (**Neon Console → your project → Postgres database → Data API → enable, choosing Managed Better Auth**).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kureemn/berkeley-network-tracker.git
cd berkeley-network-tracker
npm install

cp .env.example .env.local
# Fill in NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_DATA_API_URL, and
# DATABASE_URL from the Neon Console (Data API page + Connection Details).

npm run db:migrate   # applies db/schema.sql: table, RLS policies, grants
npm run dev           # http://localhost:3000
```

Run the test suite and a production build at any time:

```bash
npm test     # Vitest — validation unit tests
npm run build
```

## Environment variables

See [`.env.example`](.env.example) for the full list with placeholder values. Names only, no real secrets, ever:

| Variable | Exposed to browser? | Used by this app? |
|---|---|---|
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL` | Yes | Yes — the Managed Better Auth endpoint the browser talks to directly. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_DATA_API_URL` | Yes | Yes — the Data API (PostgREST) endpoint the browser talks to directly. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | No | Only by `db/migrate.mjs`, run locally/by hand to apply `db/schema.sql`. The deployed app never reads it, and it is not set in Vercel. |
| `NEON_AUTH_BASE_URL` | No | Not used by this implementation (it's the base URL a server-side Better Auth proxy would use). Documented in `.env.example` in case that's added later. |
| `NEON_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` | No | Same as above — reserved, not used. |

Because authentication and data access both happen client-side against Neon's own services, the Postgres connection string is never loaded by the running application at all — it only ever touches a local shell (or CI secret) when someone runs the migration script. `.env.local` is git-ignored; only `.env.example` is committed.

text:
## Database schema

Full DDL lives in [`db/schema.sql`](db/schema.sql). The `contacts` table:

| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `uuid` | Primary key, `default gen_random_uuid()`. |
| `user_id` | `text` | **Not null**, `default auth.user_id()`. Owning user's id, taken from their JWT. |
| `name` | `text` | Not null; `CHECK (length(btrim(name)) > 0)` — no empty/whitespace-only names. |
| `company` | `text` | Optional. |
| `role` | `text` | Optional. |
| `met_at` | `text` | Optional — where you met them. |
| `notes` | `text` | Optional. |
| `priority` | `text` | Not null; `CHECK (priority in ('high','medium','low'))`. |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | `default now()`. |
| `updated_at` | `timestamptz` | `default now()`, kept current by an `AFTER UPDATE` trigger. |

title: Berkeley Network Tracker README
heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Authentication & Row Level Security
text:
- **Four separate policies**, one per operation, rather than one blanket policy — each is independently readable and testable, and matches the assignment's requirement of distinct select/insert/update/delete policies.
- **`update` has both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`.** `USING` gates which existing rows you're even allowed to touch; `WITH CHECK` re-evaluates the same predicate against the row *after* the write. Without `WITH CHECK`, a user could `UPDATE ... SET user_id = 'someone-else'` and hand a row off to another account. With it, that write is rejected because the row would no longer satisfy `auth.user_id() = user_id`.
- **RLS is necessary but not sufficient.** Postgres also checks table-level `GRANT`s before it ever consults a policy — RLS policies restrict *which rows*, grants control *whether the role can attempt the operation at all*. Both are required; the last line above grants the `authenticated` role permission on all four operations.

title: Berkeley Network Tracker README
heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Authentication & Row Level Security
text:
- **The frontend holds no elevated credentials.** `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_DATA_API_URL` are safe to ship to the browser precisely because every request they make is authenticated as a specific end user and constrained by the policies above — there is no service-role key anywhere in this app.
- **Validation is layered.** The `CHECK` constraints on `name` and `priority` are the actual, unbypassable enforcement — they apply no matter how a row is written. The Zod schema in `lib/validation.ts` mirrors the same rules purely so the UI can show an inline error instantly instead of round-tripping to Postgres first.

## Deployment

1. Neon: create a project, then **Postgres database → Data API → Enable**, choosing **Managed Better Auth** as the auth provider (or `neonctl data-api create --auth-provider neon_auth`). This provisions the `auth` schema, `auth.user_id()`, and the `authenticated` / `anonymous` Postgres roles.
2. Apply the schema: `npm run db:migrate` (runs `db/schema.sql` against `DATABASE_URL`).
3. Push the repo to GitHub, then import it into Vercel (or `vercel link && vercel deploy --prod`).
4. In Vercel, add `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_DATA_API_URL` as environment variables (Production, Preview, and Development).
5. Add the deployed Vercel domain to Neon Auth's trusted origins: `neonctl neon-auth domain add https://your-app.vercel.app` (or via the Neon Console).
6. Open the live URL in a private browser window and run through the [verification checklist](#authentication--row-level-security) above.

heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Known limitations & next steps
text:
## Known limitations & next steps

- **Client-side route guards, not server-side.** Because auth state lives in the browser (Managed Better Auth issues a JWT the SDK holds client-side) rather than in a Next.js-readable cookie, `/contacts` is protected by a client-side redirect (`lib/neon/use-auth-guard.ts`) rather than server middleware. This is a UX guard, not the security boundary — the real boundary is Postgres RLS, which holds regardless of what the client does.
- **No password reset / email verification flow** — out of scope for this assignment, but Managed Better Auth supports both and they'd be a natural next addition.
- **Client-side search/filter only operates on the currently loaded page** of contacts, which is fine at personal-networking scale (dozens to low hundreds of contacts) but wouldn't scale to a huge list without server-side pagination and search.
- **No contact photos or richer fields** (LinkedIn URL, tags, last-contacted date) — deliberately kept to the fields the assignment specifies.
- **Single Neon branch/environment** — a production app would likely add a preview/staging branch via Neon's branching before promoting schema changes.

# Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission

I trained Karpathy's actual nanoGPT (2 blocks, 4 heads, 64-number embeddings, 48-token
context, word tokens) from scratch **twice**, and evaluated each model on the fixed
48-case language suite before and after training:

1. **Experiment 1, starter corpus:** the notebook's synthetic classroom sentences only.
2. **Experiment 2, expanded corpus:** the same sentences plus 1,565 teaching sentences I
   wrote for four extension categories: **grammar, opposites, everyday knowledge,
   categories/analogies**.

Steps (3,000), learning rate (0.001), seed, model size and eval suite were identical, so
**the corpus is the only thing that changed**.

Local, Python 3.12 (tested on an Apple M1 Pro, CPU):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kureemn/custom-llm-submission.git
```


text:
### Why these four categories

The notebook's chunker splits text at every `. ` (`re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+|\n+")`), so
**every sentence becomes its own training passage**:

```text
chunk_text("the cup is not green . it is yellow . the cup is yellow .")
→ ['the cup is not green .', 'it is yellow .', 'the cup is yellow .']
```

Negation, reference, sequence and spatial evals all depend on a fact stated in an
*earlier sentence*, such as "the box is not red . it is blue . the box is". The model never
sees tokens after a "." inside a training passage, so no teaching file can show it that
pattern without changing the pipeline. Grammar, opposites and everyday knowledge are
**single-sentence** prompts, so the pipeline *can* teach them. The starter lacks their
vocabulary entirely (*bird*, *opposite*, *water*, *umbrella*…). I added
**categories/analogies** as a deliberate probe: its prompts have two sentences, and I
predicted the model would learn the facts but fail to use them after a preceding sentence.
The [probes](#why-it-passed-or-failed-mechanism-probes) confirm this.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
section: Design rules: teaching the skill without copying the exam
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > Corpus sources, permissions and the extension design > Design rules: teaching the skill without copying the exam
text:
1. **Test items only in alternate phrasings.** hot/cold, empty/full, noisy/quiet,
   water/ice, umbrella/dry, dark/light, salmon/fish, apple/fruit and kitten/cat appear only
   in contrasts, descriptions and "one kind of" sentences, never in the eval's own frame.
2. **Eval frames only with other items, and never completed with that eval's answer *or*
   distractors.** *the opposite of big is small* is taught, but no "opposite" sentence uses
   hot, cold, fast, early or soft. *to hear music we turn on a radio* is taught, but no
   *turn on* sentence ends in light, pillow, spoon or shoe. That way the teaching data cannot
   nudge any particular choice. Grammar is the one exception, because the frame *is* the rule.
   Even there, the eval's subjects never appear in the frame: no "one bird", no "the dogs",
   no "yesterday she".
3. **Small, reused vocabulary.** The notebook keeps only the 509 most frequent training
   types. My first draft had 580 combined types, so rare eval words like *robin* and
   *freezes* would have become `<UNK>`. I rewrote it around a shared lexicon: **463
   combined types**, and every eval word appears in ≥ 5 passages.

text:
### One real gradient and weight update

The notebook saved coordinate 0 of `customer`'s embedding across the very first AdamW step:

| Run | Before | Gradient | Learning rate at step 1 | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Exp. 1 | −0.0575919 | **+0.000693** | 0.00001 | −0.0576019 | −0.0000100 |
| Exp. 2 | −0.0164004 | **−0.001230** | 0.00001 | −0.0163904 | +0.0000100 |

- **The gradient** is ∂loss/∂weight on the first batch. A positive gradient says "increasing
  this number would increase the loss".
- **The step size** is 0.001 × 1/100, because warmup starts the learning rate at 1% of its peak.
- **The update moves against the gradient's sign:** down when the gradient is positive (Exp. 1), up
  when it is negative (Exp. 2).
- **The size is exactly the learning rate, even though the two gradients differ by almost
  2×.** On Adam's first step, the normalized update m̂/√v̂ equals g/|g| = ±1. So every
  parameter moves by ≈ lr regardless of gradient size. AdamW's decoupled weight decay
  (0.01 × lr × weight ≈ 6e‑9) is negligible here.
- **Plain SGD would behave differently:** lr × gradient would move this weight by only 7e‑9.

### Next-token probabilities for the same prefix

Prefix **`the customer`** ([`inspection.json`](llm_runs/20260921T061558_478156Z/inspection.json)):

| Run | Before training (top 5) | After training (top 6) |
|---|---|---|
| Exp. 1 | customer 0.016, bus 0.011, educator 0.010, us 0.010, application 0.010 (≈ uniform 1/136 = 0.0074) | reviewed 0.178, recommended 0.171, ordered 0.169, selected 0.163, compared 0.160, returned 0.143 |
| Exp. 2 | customer 0.004, bottle 0.003, under 0.003, compared 0.003, data 0.003 (≈ 1/465) | compared 0.202, selected 0.179, recommended 0.168, reviewed 0.149, returned 0.143, ordered 0.141 |

After training, about 98% of the probability sits on exactly the six verbs the corpus uses
after "the customer", split almost evenly (≈ 1/6 each). The corpus chooses among those
verbs at random, so no model can do better than about 1/6 here. **That is why the loss
cannot reach 0**, and why it plateaus around 0.7.

heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > Learning evidence > Attention uses earlier context only
text:
### Attention uses earlier context only

Block 1, head 1, at the last position of `the customer` (the row that predicts the next
word): Exp. 1 attends **BOS 0.485, the 0.423, customer 0.092**; Exp. 2 attends 0.385 /
0.397 / 0.218. A causal mask sets future positions to −∞ before the softmax, so each row
sums to 1 over *earlier and current* tokens only. A prediction can never see the word it is
trying to predict. The later probes show attention's power and its limit. It can reach back
to "hot" several words earlier and produce "cold". But in two-sentence prompts, it also
reaches back to the *first* sentence's category and copies it.

### Temperature changes sampling, not weights

[`temperature_comparison.json`](llm_runs/20260921T062609_432761Z/temperature_comparison.json):
same trained weights, same seed, same starting token (BOS).

| T | Experiment 2 samples |
|---|---|
| 0.3 | *the team discussed the dentist and the treatment at the hospital .* · *the report about the buyer explains the purchase in detail .* · *the important client was mentioned in the order report yesterday .* · *the important bicycle was mentioned in the travel report yesterday .* |
| 0.8 | *today the hospital focused on care and the important nurse .* · *a review of harvest helped us understand the new pear .* · *every day she she plays outside .* · *a review of return helped us understand the local bond .* |
| 1.2 | ***coffee is many up gets .*** · *a review of route helped us understand the important bus .* · *right now they are over the house .* · *one boy is happy , but the song is sad .* |

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > Learning evidence > Temperature changes sampling, not weights
text:
Sampling divides the logits by T before the softmax:
- **T < 1** sharpens the distribution toward the top token. At 0.3 the samples are the most
  common template, and the least varied.
- **T > 1** flattens it, so rare tokens get sampled. At 1.2 the model produced the
  ungrammatical *coffee is many up gets*.

Experiment 1's 0.8 and 1.2 samples were **identical**
([file](llm_runs/20260921T061558_478156Z/temperature_comparison.json)). Its template-only
model is so confident (often p > 0.95 per token) that flattening rarely changes which token
the fixed random draw lands on. Temperature only matters where the model is genuinely
uncertain. No weights change at any temperature.

## The 48 fixed language evals

**Scoring (unchanged course runner):**
1. Feed only the prompt to the model.
2. Compare the next-token probabilities of the four answer choices. The highest wins; a tie scores 0.

seed. The free text is **not** what gets scored. Suite SHA‑256
`e8affcd72841e3ed7da5c0b6b116327fe9f69c9abd66a1180d1d88ceaa3e17f7` is identical in all four

text:
### Four-choice score vs free continuation

They often disagree, and the difference matters:
- **Starter place prompts (lang_09–16):** the right word has p ≈ 0.96, and the free text
  says it too (*"store ."*). These are real learned associations.
- **Opposites (lang_28–30):** the answer is the top token, and the free continuation is
  exactly the answer (*"cold ."*, *"full ."*, *"quiet ."*).
- **lang_20 *fruit*, lang_24 *delivery*:** counted correct, but the correct word has
  probability 1e‑5 to 1e‑4 and rank 157 and 28. The free text says *"market ."* and
  *"different merchandise ."*. The model would never actually say the answer; it just
  ranked it above three even less likely words. **In Experiment 1, three of the four
  "correct" new-wording cases were like this** (fruit, route, delivery: every choice ≈ 1e‑5).
  Only *health* (0.16) was a real win.
- **lang_45 *light*** wins 0.020 against *spoon* 0.013, but the model's real answer is
  *"fan ."*. Its training frame "to cool the room we turn on a fan" is louder than the
  dark → light fact.

### What changed, and is it vocabulary or learned patterns?

The overall change is +12 correct (20 → 32). Four different things happened:

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
section: What changed, and is it vocabulary or learned patterns?
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > The 48 fixed language evals > What changed, and is it vocabulary or learned patterns?
text:
- **+0 from starter patterns.** They stayed at 16/16 even though classroom text is now only
  about 75% of each batch.
- **+4 from new wording (4/8 → 8/8): patterns, not vocabulary.** All 8 cases were already
  scorable. In Experiment 1, 7 of the 8 had near-zero probability (≈ 1e‑5) for every
  choice. The prompts change the template's subject ("*our hospital* discussed…"), and a
  template-only model was lost. The exception was lang_17, *health* 0.16. In Experiment 2, lang_17/18/19/23 put real mass on the answer (0.07–0.18).
  *My interpretation, not proven:* the extension's varied subjects ("yesterday the girl…",
  "the farmer uses…") made the model less bound to "the team discussed". lang_20/21/22/24
  are still weak wins, and **none** of the 8 is a strict top‑1 answer in either run.
- **+8 from extension cases (0 → 8): vocabulary first, then patterns.** Coverage was
  necessary but not sufficient. The untrained expanded model had the same coverage and got
  6/12 by luck. Training made 4 of the 8 strict top‑1 answers: *is*, *cold*, *full*,
  *quiet*. Only the weights changed between those two measurements, so those 4 are learned
  patterns.

What this shows:

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
section: Why it passed or failed: mechanism probes
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > The 48 fixed language evals > Why it passed or failed: mechanism probes
text:
- **Opposites passed through real composition, but not "understanding".** The
  "the opposite of X is" frame was never taught with hot/cold. Yet the model answers
  cold, and it transfers to pairs it never saw in the frame (cold → hot, fast → slow).
  However, *"the soup is hot **and** the tea is"* also gives **cold 0.86**. The model
  learned "after *is*, produce the contrast partner of an earlier adjective". It ignores
  whether the sentence says *but*, *and* or *opposite*.
- **Category failure = cross-sentence context (the chunker).** The model *knows* salmon is
  a fish (0.26) and apple is a fruit (0.74) when asked in one sentence. The same question
  after a preceding sentence collapses to *farm* and *kitchen*. It has never seen a passage
  continue after a ".". The two "correct" category answers are weak wins (p = 0.017,
  0.007). And *kitten grows into a* fails even alone, because *cat* was never a
  "grows into a" completion (rule 2) and the model did not transfer kitten → cat into
  that frame.
- **"the dogs" failed because of how I constrained the data.** To avoid leakage, "dogs"
  never followed "the" and never preceded "are", so it appeared in only 7 sentences. Two of

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
section: Why it passed or failed: mechanism probes
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > The 48 fixed language evals > Why it passed or failed: mechanism probes
text:
those are "two dogs **were** playing" and "many dogs **were** running". The model learned
  dogs ↔ *past tense* (were 0.76), so among is/am/was/are it picked the past form **was**.
  The plural rule transferred to a well-represented noun (*the cats* → are 0.96) but not to
  a rare one. This is a real side effect of my own leakage rules.
- **Knowledge failures: the facts are learned, but bound to the taught shape.** The water
  fact works in its taught form (*ice 0.97*). But "water freezes into" → **the** 0.97,
  because the grammar file contains "**into the**" 36 times ("jumped into the lake"),
  and that frame dominates. Likewise *an umbrella keeps the girl* → **dry**, while "…to stay" → cool/warm,
  because the tools frame taught *stay warm / stay cool*.

**Conclusion:** coverage was the gate. After that, the model succeeded exactly when the
eval's wording matched a mechanism it had learned (contrast partner, agreement for common
nouns). It failed when the wording triggered a different, more frequent frame, or needed
cross-sentence context. More training steps would not fix these failures. Changing the
data (and the chunker) would.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
## What I learned

> My own answers, with the values from my two runs as support.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
1. **What my corpus can teach, and why I held data back.** My corpus is the passages I
   trained on: 6,157 short sentences, 4,592 generated by the notebook and 1,565 I wrote
   myself. What it really teaches the model is **which words follow which** — the
   associations between words. It can't teach anything I didn't write down, and it can't
   use a word outside the 465 in its vocabulary. That shows up directly in the evals: 12 of
   the 48 cases couldn't even be scored, because their words never appear in my text. I
   held 10% of the passages back because **training loss only tells me how well the model
   fits sentences it has already seen**. The held-out passages never produced a gradient,
   so the fact that they score close to the training ones (0.903 vs 0.787) tells me it
   learned the patterns instead of memorizing individual sentences. It is still a weak
   test, because my held-out sentences reuse the same templates as the training ones.
2. **Token, ID, vector, embedding.** The token is the piece of text itself, like
   *customer*. The **ID tells the model which row to look up** — it is just an address. The

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
vector is the 64 numbers stored in that row, and the embedding table is all 465 rows of
   them. My clearest evidence that the ID means nothing on its own: *customer* was ID 28 in
   Experiment 1 and ID 102 in Experiment 2. Same word, different row number, because I
   added words earlier in the alphabet. The numbers in the row are what carry the meaning,
   and those are what training changed: the vector grew from length 0.158 to 0.620, and its
   closest neighbours went from random words to *shopper, client, buyer*.
3. **Why it's a neural network, and how it learned.** It is a neural network because it is
   built from layers of **weighted sums**, and those weights are **learned from the data**
   rather than written by me — 132,928 of them here. Training is a loop: the model predicts
   what comes next, the loss says how wrong that prediction was, and the weights change a
   little to make better predictions next time. In numbers: the loss started at 6.19, which
   is just guessing (ln 465 ≈ 6.14), and ended at 0.79. The first update I saved shows one
   step of the loop: the gradient on `customer[0]` was +0.000693, and the weight moved

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
−0.00001, against the gradient's direction. Repeat that for every weight, 3,000 times.
4. **What attention combines, and why it can't see ahead.** The model's whole job is
   predicting the next word, so **it can't be allowed to see that word** — if it could, there
   would be nothing to learn and the loss would go to zero without the model understanding
   anything. What it can do is look back. A word's meaning depends on what came before it,
   so attention looks at the earlier words to get context. At the last position of
   `the customer`, the first head puts 0.485 on `<BOS>`, 0.423 on *the* and 0.092 on
   *customer* — it is reading the earlier words, and the causal mask blocks everything
   after.
5. **How probabilities become text, and what temperature does.** The model writes **one
   word at a time**. At each step it produces a probability for every word that could come
   next, one is picked, added to the sentence, and the process repeats. Temperature shapes
   how that pick is made: **low is repetitive, high is more random**. At 0.3 my model wrote
   only its most common templates; at 1.2 it wrote *coffee is many up gets .* Nothing was

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
retrained between those samples — same weights, same seed, only the sampling changed.
6. **Did it match my predictions, and what can I honestly conclude?** My conclusion is that
   **this small model learns the patterns that are in the data I gave it, and is mostly
   matching what it has seen**. Most of my predictions held: the losses, the neighbours of
   *customer*, the vocabulary coverage (36/48) and grammar all landed where I expected.
   Two surprises: opposites scored 3/3 when I predicted about 1/3, and the everyday
   knowledge cases failed for a different reason than I guessed — the model had learned the
   facts, but only in the sentence shape I taught them in. So a 66.7% score is not evidence
   that this model understands language. It is a public benchmark I could read while
   designing the corpus, on a model that answers well only when the wording matches what it
   was trained on.
7. **Two failures I can explain, and what they taught me.**
   - **"the dogs" → *was*.** This one is my own doing. To keep the test out of my training
     data, I never let "dogs" follow "the" and never let "are" follow "dogs". That left the

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > What I learned
text:
word in only 7 sentences, and 2 of them say "two dogs **were** playing". So the model
     learned that *dogs* goes with past tense, not that *dogs* is plural, and it picked
     *was* out of is/am/was/are. The plural rule itself did get learned — "the cats" gives
     *are* at 96% — just not for a word it barely saw. Rare words don't inherit a rule.
   - **"a salmon is a" → *bird*.** On its own, the model answers this correctly: *fish* at
     0.26. The eval puts one sentence in front of it ("a robin is a bird ."), and the
     answer collapses to *farm*. The reason is in the pipeline: the notebook splits text at
     every ".", so each sentence becomes its own training passage and the model never once
     saw words continue after a period. It knows the fact and cannot use it across a
     sentence boundary. That is the single change I would make next.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > Limitation and next experiment
text:
## Limitation and next experiment

**Observed limitation:** the model cannot use information from an earlier sentence. The
cause is the pipeline, not model capacity: `chunk_text` turns every sentence into its own
passage. The model knows *a salmon is a* → fish and *an apple is a* → fruit. It even
generalizes *a trout is a* → fish from a sentence it never trained on. Yet all three break
as soon as another sentence comes first. The same limitation is why negation, reference,
sequence and spatial remain 0/12, as unscorable (and unteachable) cases.

**Proposed next experiment:** change one thing, the chunker. Pack consecutive sentences
from the same line into one passage, up to 47 tokens, and only split at line breaks. The
classroom corpus is one sentence per line, so its passages would be byte-identical. Then:
- add multi-sentence teaching stories for negation and reference (*"the cup is not green
  . it is yellow . the cup is yellow ."*, with different objects from the evals);
- give *dogs* ordinary present-tense plural contexts ("many dogs play", "some dogs sleep");
- rerun the same 48 cases.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM README
heading_path: Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission > Limitation and next experiment
text:
**Prediction:** the two-sentence category cases should recover to the one-sentence
probabilities (fish/fruit as top‑1), negation and reference should become scorable, and
some should become correct. The model is still small, so I would expect the
correction-pattern cases to be harder than simple recall.

text:
## My three choices

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Exploration** | `0.10` | Evaluation runs at 5% exploration, so training at 20% put the agent in a noticeably noisier world than the one it is graded in. In Ms. Pac-Man a single random step into a ghost ends a life, so a high constant epsilon both suppresses scores and pollutes replay with deaths the policy did not choose. 10% keeps genuine exploration while staying closer to evaluation conditions. Measured directly: run 2 at 0.20 scored 768; run 3 at 0.10 scored 1032. |
| **Episodes** | `800` | Training is fast on this hardware (~11 episodes/minute), so episode budget was the cheapest lever available. Earlier runs showed 100 episodes was far too short to generalize (+12 points) and 400 was still improving at the end. 800 episodes gave 122,849 learning updates — enough for the policy to consolidate rather than just track recent experience. |

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > My three choices
text: | **Learning rate** | `0.0001` | Kept at the notebook's reference value. The failure mode in my first run was *instability* — training score rising while evaluation score stayed flat — not slow learning, and raising the learning rate on an unstable setup generally makes it worse. Holding this fixed across all three runs also kept the comparison between them interpretable. |

section: Two other hyperparameters I changed, and why
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > My three choices > Two other hyperparameters I changed, and why
text:
### Two other hyperparameters I changed, and why

The assignment permits tuning other settings with an explanation. I changed two, both in response to
evidence from run 1 rather than guesswork:

| Setting | Stock | Mine | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REPLAY_CAPACITY` | 5,000 | **15,000** | Run 1 averaged ~612 decisions per episode, so a 5,000-transition buffer held barely 8 games. The network was learning almost entirely from its own recent behavior, which is how run 1 produced a rising training score alongside a flat evaluation score. 15,000 retains roughly 25 games. |
| `TARGET_EVERY` | 1,000 | **2,000** | The target network supplies the "correct answer" each update aims at. Syncing every 1,000 decisions moved that target roughly every 1.6 episodes, so the network was chasing a shifting goalpost. The DQN paper uses 10,000 steps at full Atari scale; 2,000 is a middle ground suited to this shorter budget. |

**Evaluation settings were not touched.** The same five seeds (`101, 202, 303, 404, 505`), 5%
evaluation exploration, and the 3,000-decision cap apply identically before and after training, as
the assignment requires.

section: What I expected, and what actually happened
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > What I expected, and what actually happened
text:
## What I expected, and what actually happened

**Before training I expected** a modest but clear improvement over the untrained baseline, and I
expected the training score curve to be the place where I would see it — a line that rises steadily
as the agent gets better, with the final evaluation confirming what the curve already showed.

**What actually happened** was different in three ways, and each one was more informative than the
result I expected:

1. **The training curve is a poor proxy for the graded score.** In run 1 the training score climbed
   from ~450 to ~750 while the evaluation mean moved just +12. In the submitted run the training
   average *fell* from 882 (episodes 1-100) to ~700 mid-run before recovering to 887, while the
   evaluation score more than doubled. Training runs at 10% exploration and evaluation at 5%, so the
   two measure different things; only the five-seed evaluation counts.

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
section: What I expected, and what actually happened
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > What I expected, and what actually happened
text:
2. **The loss went up, not down.** Mean update loss rose from 0.02 to about 0.14 and plateaued. An
   untrained network predicts near-zero values for every move, which is trivially self-consistent and
   produces tiny errors. As the agent learned that pellets and ghosts genuinely carry value, its
   Q-values grew in magnitude and so did the absolute error between prediction and target. Rising
   loss here reflects the scale of what is being learned, not failure — the assignment's warning that
   lower loss does not mean better play turned out to be inverted in my run.

3. **I misjudged a mid-run dip as degradation.** Around episode 250-350 the 25-game average dropped
   roughly 30% below its earlier peak and I read it as the policy collapsing. It was noise: episodes
   601-800 were the strongest blocks of the entire run (means of 910 and 887, including a single game
   scoring 4,400). With per-episode scores ranging from 130 to 4,400, even 50- and 100-episode
   windows are rough estimates.

section: How the agent works, in plain language
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > How the agent works, in plain language
text:
## How the agent works, in plain language

**What it observes.** The agent never sees the game the way a person does. Each screen is shrunk to
an 84 × 84 grayscale image, and **four consecutive screens are stacked** into one observation. Four
screens rather than one because a single frozen image cannot show which way anything is moving — from
one picture you cannot tell whether a ghost is coming toward you or away. One "decision" covers four
emulator frames.

**What it can do.** Nine joystick actions: do nothing, the four directions, and the four diagonals.
That is the agent's entire vocabulary. It has no concept of a pellet, a ghost, or a maze — only
pixels in, one of nine moves out.

**How it is rewarded.** The game's own points are the reward: pellets, power pellets, fruit, and
eaten ghosts. During learning these rewards are clipped to the range −1 to +1 so that one enormous
payoff cannot dominate every update, but **every score reported in this README is the raw game
score**. Nobody tells the agent that ghosts are dangerous or that pellets are good; it infers all of
it from points arriving after certain moves.

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
section: How the agent works, in plain language
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > How the agent works, in plain language
text:
**How it learns.** A convolutional network estimates the future value of each of the nine moves.
The agent mostly picks its highest-valued move and occasionally moves at random. Experiences go into
a replay memory, and batches of 32 are sampled from it to adjust the network toward
`reward + 0.99 × (value of what came next)`, where a second, slower-updating copy of the network
supplies that second term.

---

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > One limitation
text:
## One limitation

**Five evaluation games is too small a sample to rank agents confidently.** My own results show why:
the per-episode training scores in this run ranged from 130 to 4,400, so a single game says
very little. The gap between run 2 (768) and run 3 (1032) rests on five games per condition, and
seed 101 barely moved even in the winning run. I believe the improvement is real because it shows up
on four of five independent seeds and across two successive runs, but the *precise* mean is not a
stable quantity, and small differences between two agents on this protocol should not be treated as
meaningful. Anything close to this score is, for practical purposes, a tie.

A second, narrower limitation worth recording: `ReplayMemory.sample()` calls
`rng.sample(list(self.items), size)`, which copies the entire replay deque on every sampling call.
Raising replay capacity to 15,000 therefore cut throughput from about 200 to 114 decisions per
second — the tuning that improved learning also made each run substantially slower.

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > One next experiment
text:
## One next experiment

**Change only the exploration rate, from 0.10 to 0.05, and keep episodes at 800 and the learning rate
at 0.0001.**

Exploration is the setting with the clearest evidence behind it: holding everything else fixed,
dropping it from 0.20 to 0.10 took the mean from 768 to 1032. That is a single data point on a trend,
and the obvious question is whether the trend continues or reverses. 0.05 would match the evaluation
condition exactly, so the agent would train in the same world it is graded in.

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN README
heading_path: Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission > One next experiment
text:
I genuinely do not know which way it goes, which is why it is worth running. Lower exploration could
keep helping for the reason 0.10 helped — fewer random steps into ghosts, cleaner replay data. Or it
could hurt: with only 5% random moves and no epsilon decay, the agent may stop encountering states
its current policy avoids, reinforcing its own blind spots. Seed 101 is the case to watch — it scored
360 against a 350 baseline in the winning run, and it was also the weakest seed in run 1, so there may
be a situation in that game this agent does not learn to handle. Less exploration would plausibly make
that worse, and that failure is more informative than another point of mean score.

# Berkeley Networking Tracker

This application is a private contact tracker designed for Berkeley users, ensuring that each user can only view their own contacts. Security is enforced primarily by Postgres Row Level Security (RLS), which restricts data access based on the user's JWT. The application uses a modern stack including Next.js, Neon Postgres, and Neon Managed Better Auth for authentication and data access.

heading_path: Berkeley Networking Tracker > Key facts
text:
## Key facts

- Every visitor signs in with their own account, and every row in the database is invisible to everyone except the person who created it. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Berkeley Networking Tracker|Berkeley Networking Tracker]])
- Priority is restricted to `high` / `medium` / `low` — enforced in Postgres, not just the UI. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Features|Features]])
- The Frontend is a deliberately "thin" frontend, rendering UI and validating input for instant feedback. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Architecture|Architecture]])
- The `contacts` table has a `user_id` column defaulting to `auth.user_id()` from the JWT. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Database schema|Database schema]])
- The ownership rule reduces to the predicate: `auth.user_id() = user_id`. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Authentication & Row Level Security|Authentication & Row Level Security]])
- The Data API validates JWTs and forwards requests to Postgres, which uses RLS as the security boundary. (source: [[Berkeley Network Tracker README#Architecture|Architecture]])

# Custom nanoGPT LLM

The author trained nanoGPT twice using a starter and an expanded corpus, evaluating performance on a fixed 48-case language suite. The expanded corpus, containing 1,565 synthetic teaching sentences, improved performance significantly, particularly in new wording transfer. Analysis shows the model learns patterns but is constrained by its training pipeline, especially regarding cross-sentence context.

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM
heading_path: Custom nanoGPT LLM > Key facts
text:
## Key facts

- The model was trained twice using nanoGPT with 2 blocks, 4 heads, 64-number embeddings, and 48-token context. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT Class 4 submission|Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission]])
- Experiment 2 used an expanded corpus containing the starter sentences plus 1,565 teaching sentences across four extension categories. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT Class 4 submission|Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission]])
- The expanded corpus resulted in an accuracy among scorable of 88.9% when trained, compared to 30.6% untrained. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT Class 4 submission|Building a Custom LLM with nanoGPT: Class 4 submission]])
- The model's vocabulary for Experiment 2 contained 465 unique tokens. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#The runs|The runs]])
- The author's audit showed 0 violations of 5 rules across all 48 cases regarding data leakage. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#Leakage checks|Leakage checks]])

title: Custom nanoGPT LLM
heading_path: Custom nanoGPT LLM > Key facts
text:
- The model's attention mechanism is causal, meaning it only attends to earlier and current tokens. (source: [[Custom nanoGPT LLM README#Attention uses earlier context only|Attention uses earlier context only]])

heading_path: Ms Pac-Man DQN
text:
# Ms Pac-Man DQN

The submitted run trained the DQN agent for 800 episodes, more than doubling the mean score of the untrained baseline from 492.0 to 1032.0. The agent learns by observing stacked grayscale images and receiving rewards based on in-game points. Key tuning involved setting Exploration to 0.10 and increasing Replay Capacity to 15,000.

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN
heading_path: Ms Pac-Man DQN > Key facts
text:
## Key facts

- The submitted run trained for 800 episodes and more than doubled the mean score of the untrained baseline. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission|Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission]])
- Mean score over the five evaluation games for the untrained baseline was 492.0. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission|Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission]])
- The trained agent achieved a mean score of 1032.0 over the five evaluation games. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission|Ms. Pac-Man DQN — Class 3 submission]])
- The chosen Exploration value was 0.10 to keep genuine exploration while staying closer to evaluation conditions. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#My three choices|My three choices]])
- The Learning rate was kept at 0.0001, which was the notebook's reference value. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#My three choices|My three choices]])
- REPLAY_CAPACITY was increased from 5,000 to 15,000 because a 5,000-transition buffer held barely 8 games. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#Two other hyperparameters I changed, and why|Two other hyperparameters I changed, and why]])

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN
heading_path: Ms Pac-Man DQN > Key facts
text:
- The mean update loss rose from 0.02 to about 0.14 and plateaued, reflecting the scale of what is being learned. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#What I expected, and what actually happened|What I expected, and what actually happened]])
- The total elapsed time for the run was 4,388 seconds (~73 minutes) on an Apple M1 Pro. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#What the run actually cost|What the run actually cost]])
- The agent observes four consecutive screens stacked into one observation, which is 84 × 84 grayscale. (source: [[Ms Pac-Man DQN README#How the agent works, in plain language|How the agent works, in plain language]])

title: Ms Pac-Man DQN
heading_path: Ms Pac-Man DQN > Concepts and tools used
text:
## Concepts and tools used

- [[Deep Q-Network]]: The agent uses a convolutional network to estimate the future value of each of the nine moves.
- [[Replay Memory]]: Experiences go into a replay memory, and batches of 32 are sampled from it to adjust the network.
- [[Exploration]]: Training exploration was lowered from 0.20 to 0.10 because evaluation runs at 5% exploration; the run at 0.10 scored 1032 versus 768 at 0.20.
- [[Learning Rate]]: The learning rate was kept at the notebook's reference value to maintain interpretability across runs.
- [[PyTorch]]: The run utilized the PyTorch MPS backend on the Apple M1 Pro hardware.
